breadcrumb.name: UPS vs Solar vs Generator: Cost per Backup Hour Over Five Years

sections.h2: Which is the cheapest backup for loadshedding?
p: With the defaults, 600 W for 4 hours a day over 5 years, the answer is UPS at Rs 600,665 in total. The UPS comes to Rs 600,665, hybrid solar to Rs 609,785 and the generator to Rs 1,622,690; solar has no running cost once bought, the generator pays for petrol every hour.

The answer can change with the load and the hours. For 300 W over 2 hours a day the cheapest is UPS (Rs 208,633 over 5 years); hybrid solar still has to buy a whole lithium pack and an inverter however small the load. Enter your own load and hours above.

A petrol generator runs its engine for every hour of backup, and even lightly loaded it burns a large share of its full-load fuel. At Rs 382.02 a litre that is Rs 272,211 a year here, plus Rs 25,137 of engine oil at one change every 100 running hours. Our fuel curve is fitted to inverter generators, so an open-frame set burns somewhat more and costs more than shown.

A UPS only pays for the units it takes back from the grid, which are more than it delivers because of charger and inverter losses: 1,213 units, Rs 44,211 a year. Its real cost is the batteries, replaced every 3 years. Its charger must also refill the batteries between cuts: the calculator checks this with a 25 A charger and leaves a UPS that cannot keep up out of the cheapest, which happens with big loads or very long cuts.

sections.h2: What the hybrid solar figure includes
p: The smallest hybrid inverter in our price data that carries the load and is built for the lithium pack's battery voltage, lithium batteries in whole packs for one night's backup, and enough panels to refill the battery on an average day in your city, never fewer than the string a hybrid inverter needs to start: a hybrid inverter for the lithium pack switches on only when the panels in series give about 150 V, and works from about 120 V, which on a hot afternoon takes 4 panels of 585 W. It assumes the sun recharges the battery, so a run of cloudy days would still need the grid.

It does not count the bill savings solar makes during the day. The Home Power Planner on our home page does: it prices the same backup with on-grid or hybrid solar for your whole appliance list and its bill, so its pick can differ from the one here. It also leaves out mounting, cabling and installation (they add to every option, most to solar), the inverter's own standby draw and grid charging on cloudy days.

Every figure is the middle of a price range from Pakistani retailer listings or our solar price tracker, equipment only, each listed under Sources with its publisher. Retailer prices for the same model differ a lot, so replace them with your own quotes before you decide.
Battery lives are planning values: tubular 3 years and lithium 8 years. Heat, deep discharges and poor charging shorten both.

faq.q: Which is cheaper for loadshedding: UPS, solar or generator?
faq.a: It depends on the load and the hours. For 600 W through 4 hours a day over 5 years, UPS is cheapest at Rs 82 per backup hour; for 300 W through 2 hours the cheapest is UPS at Rs 57.

faq.q: How much does a petrol generator cost per hour?
faq.a: For 600 W on a 2.5 kVA set, about 0.49 litres an hour, Rs 272,211 of petrol a year at 4 hours a day, plus oil. With the purchase spread over 5 years that is Rs 222 per backup hour.

faq.q: How much does it cost to recharge a UPS battery?
faq.a: The units a UPS takes from the grid are its backup units divided by the charger and inverter efficiencies: 1,213 units a year for the default load, Rs 44,211 at Rs 36.46 a unit.

faq.q: How long do UPS batteries last in Pakistan?
faq.a: Tubular batteries usually last two to five years in Pakistani heat; this calculator uses 3 years. Lithium (LiFePO4) packs are rated for thousands of cycles; it uses 8 years.

faq.q: Is solar worth it only for backup?
faq.a: It depends on the load and the hours. For 300 W through 2 hours a day the cheapest backup is UPS, because even a small solar backup buys a whole lithium pack and a hybrid inverter; for 600 W through 4 hours over 5 years it is UPS. This comparison leaves out the bill savings solar makes during the day; the Home Power Planner on our home page counts them for your whole appliance list.
No. All three use equipment prices only. Installation, wiring and a changeover switch add to each, most to solar.

key_facts: Cost per backup hour = (equipment + running cost a year × years + battery replacements) ÷ hours of backup over the same years; it puts a cheap-to-buy generator and a dear-to-buy solar system on one scale.

For 600 W through 4 hours a day a petrol generator burns about 0.49 litres an hour, Rs 272,211 of petrol a year. Cheapest to buy here: petrol generator; dearest after the first year (purchase plus one year of running): hybrid solar.
A UPS takes more units from the grid than it delivers: 1,213 units a year here, Rs 44,211 at Rs 36.46 a unit, and its tubular batteries are replaced every 3 years.

For a small load and short cuts: 300 W for 2 hours a day costs Rs 57 per backup hour on a UPS against Rs 167 on hybrid solar, and the cheapest is UPS; even a small solar backup buys a whole lithium pack and a hybrid inverter built for it.
mistakes: Comparing purchase prices only. The cheapest option to buy is often the dearest to own; compare the cost per backup hour over the same years.
Forgetting battery replacements. A tubular bank is replaced every few years, and over the years the replacements can cost more than the UPS itself.
Sizing the comparison on the whole house. Backup usually runs fans, lights and a few appliances; enter only what runs during a cut.
Treating the solar total as a backup cost alone. Hybrid solar also cuts the day bill, which this comparison leaves out; installation and standby losses, also left out, work the other way.

fields.label: Load during a power cut
fields.hint: What runs together on backup: for example four fans, lights, a router and a TV. Add up the watts on the labels or use the home load calculator. Very large loads (a whole house with ACs) are beyond the UPS and generator sizes in our price list.

fields.name: surge_w
fields.label: Starting watts
fields.hint: Only if the backup runs a motor (water pump, fridge, AC): the load plus the biggest motor's extra starting watts. The UPS, generator and hybrid inverter must also start it, so each is sized for the larger of the load × margin and this. Leave blank for fans, lights and electronics.

content.answer: For 600 W through 4 hours of loadshedding a day, the cheapest backup over 5 years is UPS at about Rs 82 per backup hour: a UPS with tubular batteries costs Rs 82, hybrid solar Rs 84 and a petrol generator Rs 222. Cost = equipment + yearly running cost + battery replacements, divided by the backup hours.

formula.text: Cost per backup hour = (B + Y × R + N × P) ÷ (h × days × twelve × Y)
lines: B = equipment price (middle of the price range in our data, installation extra); Y = years compared
R = running cost a year: UPS recharge units × tariff; generator fuel (litres an hour × hours × price) + oil changes; hybrid solar none
N × P = battery replacements within the period × battery price (none in the final year of life)
Battery bank: UPS tubular Wh = load W × h ÷ (DoD × inverter efficiency); lithium kWh likewise, bought in whole packs
Generator litres an hour = no-load fuel × rated kW + fuel per kWh × load kW (the fuel calculator's curve)

content.safety: A generator needs a proper changeover switch so it can never feed the grid, and must run outdoors away from windows; a UPS or hybrid inverter connects to the house wiring at mains voltage. Have a licensed electrician fit the changeover, the inverter and the earthing for whichever option you choose.
